I have been farming this land for 35 years. I know this soil. I know this weather. My husband's brother works in the city now, so it is mostly me managing the fields with my son some weekends. I have to be practical about labor.

My 14 mu breaks like this in my head: 9 mu stays in the wheat-maize rotation like always. That is my backbone — wheat feeds us through winter, maize brings cash in autumn. The other 5 mu I split between chili and cotton. I keep a little cotton because I know how to grow it, but I am not expanding it. Picking cotton alone is hard on my back and the price has been uncertain. Chili I trust more — there is always a buyer at the local market and I know the variety I save seeds from every year.

For wheat, I buy improved seed from the village supply store like I have for the past ten years. I put down compound fertilizer when I sow, then top-dress urea at jointing. I irrigate three times: once before winter freeze, once at jointing, once at heading. That is what keeps my yield steady. I use rotary tillage after maize harvest to break up the stubble.

For maize I drill it straight into the wheat stubble — no plowing needed, saves time and diesel. Hybrid seed, always. The summer rains usually help so I only pump from the well twice unless it is a dry year.

For chili I use my own saved seed from the best plants last autumn. More water, more fertilizer. Disease can come fast so I spray four times through the season.

For cotton I stick with the hybrid Bt seed from the shop — fewer bollworm sprays needed, which matters when I am working alone.
